title: Three perfect days in Prague: piano, goose and the north bank
dek: The first St. Martin's goose menus land on Friday, a piano festival fills the Rudolfinum, and the art is up the hill in Holešovice. Here is a weekend in the Old Town, Letná and Žižkov.

hero.caption: Old Town Square and the Týn Church, where Friday's walk ends as the lamps come on.

intro:
Prague in early November is a city that has turned indoors. The light goes soon after half past four, the trees on Letná are nearly bare, and the talk in the pubs has turned to goose. St. Martin's Day falls on Wednesday, November 11, when the year's first young wines are poured, but the kitchens do not wait: from Friday, November 6, restaurants across the Old Town put roast and confit goose, goose broth and red cabbage on their menus, and most keep them for a week or more.

That gives this weekend a shape. Friday stays in the Old Town and Josefov: the synagogues of the Jewish Museum (which closes on Saturdays), a new survey of the nineteenth-century painter Jaroslav Čermák that opened on November 4, an early goose dinner, and a recital at the Rudolfinum, where the Rudolf Firkušný Piano Festival runs through Monday. Saturday crosses the river to Letná and Holešovice, the Prague 7 neighborhoods where the National Gallery keeps its modern collections in a functionalist trade-fair hall and DOX shows contemporary art in a converted factory. Sunday goes east, to Karlín's cafés, the granite memorial on Vítkov hill and the space-age TV tower in Žižkov.

Pack for cold and possible rain. Every day here has a long indoor stretch in the afternoon, and every evening ends somewhere warm.

days.title: Friday: the Old Town and Josefov
days.intro: A walking day across the old center: synagogues in the morning, a painter's rediscovery after lunch, goose before the concert.

stops.name: Grand Café Orient
stops.text: Start on the first floor of the House of the Black Madonna, the 1912 Cubist building by Josef Gočár, where the café's angled lamps, green upholstery and brass rails were all designed in the same spirit. Order coffee and the house *věneček*, the custard-filled choux pastry that here comes square rather than round, as a small joke about Cubism. **Practical:** open from 09:00 on weekdays (10:00 at weekends); the window tables look down on Celetná, the old coronation route.

stops.name: Jewish Museum in Prague
stops.text: Friday is the day for Josefov, because the museum closes every Saturday. One ticket covers the Maisel, Pinkas, Klausen and Spanish synagogues and the Old Jewish Cemetery, where centuries of headstones lean together under the trees. The Pinkas Synagogue's walls carry the hand-painted names of the Bohemian and Moravian Jews murdered in the Holocaust; give it time. The Old-New Synagogue, run separately by the Jewish community, needs its own ticket. **Practical:** winter hours are 09:00 to 16:30, and the Old-New Synagogue closes about an hour before Shabbat, so see it first.

stops.name: Alma
stops.text: A fifteen-minute walk south, past the National Theatre end of Národní, brings you to this Bib Gourmand restaurant with an open kitchen and bar and a courtyard. The cooking is contemporary rather than Czech: dry-aged beef, plenty of vegetable dishes, bread from KRO Bakery in Libeň, and a wine list worth asking about. It is a lighter lunch than the goose to come. **Practical:** open 09:00 to 18:00 on weekdays.

stops.name: Jaroslav Čermák: Myths of European Reality
stops.text: The Prague City Gallery and the National Gallery have put together the first full survey in more than a century of Čermák (1830–1878), a Czech painter who made his career in Brussels and Paris. The show follows him between those art worlds and asks how an international professional became, after his death, a symbol of Czech national painting. It opened on November 4, so you are among its first visitors. **Practical:** in the Municipal Library building; open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00; 200 CZK. The step-free entrance is on Valentinská.

stops.name: Old Town Square and the astronomical clock
stops.text: Mariánské náměstí is a two-minute walk from Old Town Square, and this is the right hour for it: the light is going, the Týn towers are lit, and the crowd under the astronomical clock is smaller than at noon. Watch the apostles at five o'clock, then walk the lanes behind the Týn Church to Liliová. **Practical:** the square is free and open; keep an eye on your phone when the crowd presses in at the top of the hour.

stops.name: V Zátiší
stops.text: One of the Old Town's established fine-dining rooms, listed in the 2026 Michelin Guide, and from November 6 to 15 it serves a St. Martin's menu: goose broth with ravioli, goose hearts and liver pâté, then roast goose with fermented red cabbage, potato noodles and currants, and apple strudel to finish. An early table gets you to the Rudolfinum on time. **Practical:** dinner service starts at 17:00; book ahead and tell them you have a 19:30 concert.

stops.name: Marek Kozák at the Rudolfinum
stops.text: The Rudolf Firkušný Piano Festival brings a recital to Dvořák Hall most nights this week. Friday belongs to the Czech pianist Marek Kozák, with a program built around the waltz and the dance: Bach's first Partita, excerpts from Smetana's Czech Dances, Ravel's *Valses nobles et sentimentales* and two Liszt showpieces ending in the Mephisto Waltz No. 1. **Practical:** the hall is a ten-minute walk from Liliová along Křižovnická. Afterward, Hemingway Bar is now at Opatovická 3, open to 02:00 on Fridays, if you want a late cocktail.

days.title: Saturday: Letná and Holešovice
days.intro: Across the river to Prague 7: a park with the best view of the bridges, two big art buildings, and Slovak cooking in an old market hall.

stops.name: Café Letka
stops.text: A neighborhood café on Letohradská that works from morning coffee to an evening beer. Come for coffee and a *koláč* or a proper brunch, and note the beer from the Matuška brewery for later in the day. **Practical:** opens at 09:00 on Saturdays; Letná Park is three minutes away on foot.

stops.name: Letná Park and the Metronome
stops.text: Walk the plateau to the giant Metronome, which stands on the plinth where a Stalin monument stood until 1962. From the terrace below it you look straight down on the Vltava and its bridges, with the Old Town spread out behind. Follow the path east along the edge of the park in the cold morning air before turning inland to Holešovice. **Practical:** free and open all day; the paths can be muddy after rain.

stops.name: Trade Fair Palace (National Gallery)
stops.text: The National Gallery's modern and contemporary collections fill this 1920s functionalist exhibition hall, and the building itself, with its vast atrium and stacked galleries, is half the reason to come. The permanent displays run from Czech modernism to the exhibition *1939–2021: The End of the Black-and-White Era*, and the gallery's 230th-anniversary interventions, including a suspended object by Jan Kaplický, stay in place until January 3. **Practical:** open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00.

stops.name: Lokál Nad Stromovkou
stops.text: A short walk west, at the edge of Stromovka park, this branch of the Lokál pubs does the Czech classics properly: *svíčková*, schnitzel, goulash and Pilsner Urquell served from tanks. It is the cheapest good meal of the weekend. **Practical:** open from 11:30; Stromovka, the old royal game park, is across the road if you want to walk lunch off before the tram to DOX.

stops.name: DOX Centre for Contemporary Art
stops.text: A converted factory with a giant wooden airship, *Gulliver*, perched on its roof. This weekend has four shows: *Argus & Medusa: On Hope in Dark Times*, David Tibet's *Hallucinate, Children*, *ANDROS*, and the last days of Radka Bodzewicz's *FAUST*, which closes on Sunday. It is a good place to spend the dark hours. **Practical:** open Tuesday to Sunday, 11:00 to 19:00.

stops.name: Skô
stops.text: Inside the Holešovice market, the red-brick former slaughterhouse, Skô cooks Slovak food over wood: *langoš*, *pagáč*, *lokše*, *halušky* and *privarok*, with house-made sausages, smoked ham and sauerkraut and a Slovak and Czech wine list. It is generous, smoky cooking for a cold night. **Practical:** dinner only, from 17:00, Monday to Saturday; reserve, because it fills up at weekends.

stops.name: Cross Club
stops.text: A ten-minute walk from the market, this club is built out of welded scrap metal, pipes and moving machine parts, and it looks even stranger in the dark. Have a drink in the café-bar or the courtyard, or stay for whatever is on the two stages. **Practical:** the club runs until 07:00 on Saturdays; there is usually a small entry fee at weekends. If you would rather hear Anna Vinnitskaya play Chopin's Third Sonata at the Rudolfinum at 19:30, take an earlier table at Skô.

days.title: Sunday: Karlín and Žižkov
days.intro: East of the center: specialty coffee in Karlín, a hill with a granite memorial, and the strangest building on the skyline.

stops.name: Můj šálek kávy
stops.text: The first café of the Prague roaster Doubleshot, and the place that taught a generation of Praguers to care where their coffee comes from. Order a filter or a coffee tasting flight and one of the breakfasts. **Practical:** opens at 10:00 on Sundays; reservations are not taken at weekends, so expect a short wait.

stops.name: National Monument at Vítkov
stops.text: Climb the wooded hill between Karlín and Žižkov to the huge equestrian statue of the Hussite general Jan Žižka and the white granite memorial behind it. Inside are the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier and an exhibition on the turning points of Czech and Czechoslovak statehood in the twentieth century, and the café has a view over the city. **Practical:** open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, last entry 17:30; admission is free.

stops.name: Eska
stops.text: Back down the hill, this bakery and restaurant serves breakfast until late afternoon and lunches built on local ingredients and its own breads: sourdough toast with scrambled eggs and smoked salmon is the classic. Buy a loaf on the way out. **Practical:** open 09:00 to 18:00 on Sundays; the bakery does not take reservations.

stops.name: Žižkov Television Tower
stops.text: Take a tram up to Žižkov for the TV tower, a 1990s rocket of a building with David Černý's giant faceless babies crawling up its legs. Go up at dusk: the observation pods look over the whole city, and you can watch the lights come on across the Old Town. **Practical:** the observation deck is open from 09:00 to midnight; adult tickets start at 350 CZK, and the desk at the bottom takes cash only, so buy online if you are paying by card.

stops.name: Výčep
stops.text: Finish fifteen minutes' walk south of the tower at this Bib Gourmand pub-restaurant, which Michelin calls an "unpretentious, modern interpretation of a traditional inn." Sit on the long benches, order the *langoš* with *bryndza* and smoked cracklings, a beer and then the *větrník*, a caramel cream pastry, for dessert. **Practical:** open until 22:00 on Sundays.

stay.name: Four Seasons Hotel Prague
stay.text: Three historic buildings on the river next to Charles Bridge, with views across to the Castle. It puts Josefov, the Rudolfinum and V Zátiší all within a short walk, which is exactly what Friday needs.

stay.name: Hotel Josef
stay.text: One of Prague's first design hotels, with glass-and-steel interiors by Eva Jiřičná and an in-house bakery. It is on Rybná, a few minutes from Old Town Square and the Jewish Museum but on a quieter street.

stay.name: Mama Shelter Prague
stay.text: A playful 238-room hotel on Veletržní, a few minutes from the Trade Fair Palace and a walk from Letná, DOX and Skô. Rooms are compact, but the lobby, bar and restaurant are lively, and the tram reaches the Old Town in minutes.

events.name: Rudolf Firkušný Piano Festival: Marek Kozák
events.text: Bach, Smetana, Ravel and Liszt from the Czech pianist, part of a festival that runs at the Rudolfinum until November 9.

events.name: Rudolf Firkušný Piano Festival: Anna Vinnitskaya
events.text: Brahms's Op. 117 Intermezzos, Rachmaninoff's Corelli Variations, Scriabin's Third Sonata and Chopin's Third Sonata.

events.name: St. Martin's goose menus begin
events.when: From Fri., through Nov. 11 to 15 depending on the restaurant
events.where: Restaurants across Prague 1, including V Zátiší, U Matěje Kotrby and Mincovna
events.text: Goose broth, confit or roast goose with red cabbage and dumplings, and from Wednesday the new St. Martin's wine. U Matěje Kotrby's menu runs November 6 to 15.

events.name: Jaroslav Čermák: Myths of European Reality
events.where: Prague City Gallery, Municipal Library building, Mariánské náměstí 1
events.text: The first comprehensive survey of the painter in over a century, from the Prague City Gallery and the National Gallery; on until February 28.

events.name: Mezipatra Queer Film Festival
events.where: Lucerna, Světozor, Edison Filmhub and Kino 35
events.text: The 27th edition brings 28 features and 50 shorts to cinemas around Wenceslas Square.

events.name: Whisky Life! Prague
events.text: Tastings, cocktails and masterclasses, some in English, in the Gothic town hall on Charles Square.

events.name: Radka Bodzewicz: FAUST closes
events.text: Last day of the exhibition, which has run at DOX since June.

know: **From the airport:** trolleybus 59 runs from Václav Havel Airport to Nádraží Veleslavín (metro line A) in about 15 minutes, and bus 100 to Zličín (line B) in about 18; both take an ordinary 90-minute ticket. The Airport Express (AE) to the main station costs 200 CZK and ordinary passes are not valid on it. A taxi, Uber or Bolt to the center usually takes 25 to 40 minutes.

**Transit:** buy tickets in the PID Lítačka app, where they are cheapest: 36 CZK for 30 minutes, 46 CZK for 90 minutes, 140 CZK for 24 hours and 340 CZK for 72 hours (paper tickets cost a little more). Activate before you board.

**St. Martin's Day:** it falls on Wednesday, November 11, when the new young wines are first poured. Goose menus start earlier, from November 6 at many restaurants, so book dinner. The big St. Martin's wine and goose festival on the Náplavka embankment is the following Saturday, November 14, not this weekend.
**Closed days:** the Jewish Museum is closed on Saturdays, so visit on Friday. Most museums, including the National Gallery, DOX, Vítkov and the Prague City Gallery, close on Mondays.
**Short days:** it is dark soon after 16:30. Do outdoor walks in the morning, and take a warm layer and an umbrella.

**Money:** the currency is the Czech koruna (CZK). Cards and phone payments work almost everywhere, but carry a little cash for market stalls and the TV tower's ticket desk. Decline offers to pay in euros.
**Tipping:** service is not usually included. Round up or add about 10 percent in restaurants and cafés, and tell the server the total you want to pay when they bring the card machine.
